title: Safety Benchmark Difficulty Stratification: Are Easy Items Doing All the Work?

original_idea.title: Safety Benchmark Difficulty Stratification: Are Easy Items Doing All the Work?
original_idea.problem: Safety benchmarks aggregate scores across items of varying difficulty, but it is unknown whether high safety scores are driven by easy items (obvious harmful requests) while hard items (subtle, context-dependent harms) are consistently failed.
original_idea.direction: Take 200-300 items from AILuminate or TrustLLM. Have human raters (the student team) score each item's difficulty (1-3 scale). Evaluate 2-3 models on all items. Disaggregate safety scores by difficulty level. Test whether models that score similarly overall differ significantly on hard items. Report a 'hard-item safety score' as a complementary metric.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If safety benchmark scores are dominated by easy items, they overstate real-world safety. Subtle, context-dependent harms are those most likely to appear in adversarial deployments. A difficulty-stratified metric is more informative.
original_idea.relevant_context: AILuminate (24K+ items) and TrustLLM are suitable datasets. Difficulty stratification is standard in capability benchmarks (e.g., Humanity's Last Exam is entirely at the hard end) but not in safety benchmarks.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: if safety scores are inflated by easy items, this directly reveals a critical gap in current safety measurement practices and motivates better metrics.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: annotating difficulty on a 1-3 scale, running models on benchmark items, and disaggregating scores are all manageable tasks for beginner CS students.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused deliverable: difficulty-stratified analysis on 200-300 items across 2-3 models with a clear 'hard-item safety score' output.

novelty.reasoning: Difficulty stratification is standard in capability benchmarks (e.g., Humanity's Last Exam) but has not been systematically applied to safety benchmarks. SALAD-Bench (ACL 2024) uses hierarchical categories but does not stratify by item difficulty with human ratings. SafetyBench (ACL 2024) has multiple-choice format but no difficulty decomposition. AIR-Bench 2024 spans 314 risk categories but aggregates scores without difficulty analysis. The specific proposal to annotate safety benchmark items by difficulty, disaggregate scores, and report a 'hard-item safety score' is mostly novel.
